_about: What each micro-topic must contain, from vault/ (syllabus + dc-motor-digest.md). topic-brief.mjs and topic-check.mjs read this. Papers are written exactly as in the digest. 'bigPicture' lists the past IOE questions the Big-picture segment must answer (one answer() or solve() video each, every role opening with that question). 'derivations' are the equations segment 2 must derive, one video each. Update this file whenever vault/ is refreshed or the user changes a topic's scope.

4.1.title: Working principle, back EMF ra torque equation
derivations: Voltage and power equation V = Eb + IaRa, Pm = EbIa
Torque equation by force Ta = 0.159 φZIa (P/A)
Torque equation by power Ta = 9.55 EbIa/N

bigPicture.q: Explain the working principle of a DC motor and derive the torque equation.
What is back EMF? How does it play an important role in a DC motor?

alsoAsked.q: How is unidirectional torque produced in a DC machine? What factors affect the torque?
Why does a DC motor draw a large current at starting?
Derive the EMF equation of a DC machine.
Numerical: EMF equation → speed, lap and wave (digest #18).

4.2.title: DC motor ka types, characteristics ra applications
syllabus: Method of excitation, Types of DC motor
derivations: Voltage and current equations of shunt, series, long and short compound motors
Shunt: Ta–Ia, N–Ia, N–Ta from Ta ∝ φIa and N ∝ Eb/φ
Series: Ta–Ia, N–Ia, N–Ta (φ ∝ Ia before saturation)

bigPicture.q: Explain the torque–armature current and speed–torque characteristics of DC shunt and DC series motors.
Why should a DC series motor never be started without load?
220 V series motor, Ra = 0.06 Ω, Rse = 0.04 Ω, 25 A at 1200 rpm. Current at 800 rpm (unsaturated)? (digest #14: I2 ≈ 37.3 A)

alsoAsked.q: Suitability of series, shunt and compound motors for traction, vacuum cleaner, paper making, shearing and punching.
Shunt motor 600 rpm, 60 A from 230 V, Ra = 0.2 Ω, Rsh = 115 Ω. Speed at Ia = 30 A? (digest #11: 615.4 rpm)
Series motor, speed at half torque (digest #15: ≈ 1147 rpm)

4.3.title: Losses ra efficiency
derivations: Power flow: input → Cu losses → Pm → iron and friction → output
Condition for maximum efficiency: variable loss = constant loss

bigPicture.q: A shunt generator delivers 30 kW at 200 V. Ra = 0.05 Ω, Rsh = 50 Ω, iron and friction losses = 1000 W: EMF, copper losses, efficiency. (digest #21: 207.7 V, 1985.8 W, 90.9%)
A shunt generator delivers 96 A at 200 V. Ra = 0.1 Ω, Rsh = 50 Ω, iron and friction losses = 2500 W: EMF and commercial efficiency. (digest #22: 210 V, 81.7%)

4.4.title: Starting: 3-point ra 4-point starter
syllabus: Starting of D.C. Motors: 3 point and 4 point starters
derivations: Why a starter: Ia = (V − Eb)/Ra with Eb = 0 at start
Starter resistance for a chosen starting current

bigPicture.q: What is the necessity of a starter? Explain the working of a 3-point starter with a neat diagram.

alsoAsked.q: Why does a DC motor draw a large current at starting?

4.5.title: Speed control: series, shunt ra direction reverse
syllabus: Speed control of D.C. motors: Field Control, Armature Control
derivations: Speed equation N ∝ Eb/φ and the ratio N2/N1 = (Eb2/Eb1)(φ1/φ2)

bigPicture.q: Explain the methods of speed control of a DC shunt motor (armature control and field control).
A 200 V shunt motor driving a constant-torque load takes 50 A at 1000 rpm. Ra = 0.1 Ω, Rsh = 100 Ω. Armature resistance for 800 rpm? (digest #8: ≈ 0.813 Ω)

4.6.title: Testing: Retardation test ra Swinburne’s test
syllabus: Losses and Efficiency (testing to find losses)
derivations: Swinburne's test: constant losses from no-load input, efficiency at any load
Retardation test: rotational losses from the slowing-down rate
4.6.gap: No Swinburne or retardation question exists in vault/. Do not invent one. Use the closest real past question (4.3 efficiency numericals, 2074 Bhadra or 2083 Baishakh ECM, solved with Swinburne's method), or ask the user for a paper.
